transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
In Israel, the vast majority of votes have been counted in yesterday's election,
but there's still a deadlock between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main challengers,
NPR's Daniel Estrin reports.
The map could still shift as the rest of the votes are counted,
but Netanyahu and his allies so far have won 53 parliamentary seats.
The center-right opposition bloc is trailing behind Netanyahu with just 48 parliamentary seats.
Neither side has the 61-seat majority they'd need.
The main question is if the center-right opposition will break campaign promises
and agree to partner with Arab-led parties.
Arab parties so far have won a record 19 seats in parliament
thanks to historically high Arab voter turnout.
Netanyahu is claiming Arab parties "stole the elections" but is not published evidence.
It's an apparent attempt to prevent the opposition from partnering with Arab parties to unseat him.
Next week, Israel's president will decide who to appoint to try to form a governing coalition.
Daniel Estrin, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
Amid high costs for a host of household expenses, many Midwesterners don't feel like home is so affordable anymore.
As the Midwest newsroom's Holly Edgel reports, voters are taking affordability into account in the midterm elections.
Rising energy, gas and housing costs pushed inflation in the Midwest several points higher than the national rate in September.
"With wages stagnant, those rising costs can really hurt," says Catherine Harvey of the nonprofit Urban Institute.
And that can leave voters feeling disaffected and fed up.
Independent Kansas voter Melanie Magana hopes the midterms mark a turning point.
"If people aren't squeezed, then maybe we could actually have happier, healthier communities."
Democratic candidate for Kansas Governor Cindy Holscher is campaigning on a hike in the minimum wage there.
It's currently $7.25 an hour.
For NPR News, I'm Holly Edgel in St. Louis.
The Federal Reserve has decided to keep interest rates steady for now, and PR Scott Horsley reports the central bank is still expected to raise rates later this year as it tries to curb inflation.
Consumer prices are still climbing much faster than the Federal Reserve would like, partly as a result of the U.S. war with Iran, which has triggered a spike in energy prices.
The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate last month in an effort to tamp down demand and slow those price hikes, but any additional rate hikes are on hold for now.
The Fed's rate-setting committee voted 10 to 2 to keep its benchmark rate where it is.
The two dissenters would have preferred to raise rates by a quarter percentage point.
The decision comes less than a week before votes are tallied in the midterm election.
President Trump has aggressively lobbied the Fed to lower interest rates.
Polls show nearly two-thirds of the public disapproves to the President's handling of the economy.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
U.S. stocks ticked higher today. This is NPR News.
A man who played a role in defrauding a federal food program in Minnesota has been sentenced to 30 years in prison.
Salim Saeed operated a restaurant that received government money for claims.
It provided thousands of meals.
President Trump has blamed Minnesota's Democratic governor for failing to catch the fraud.
Dolores Huerta, the longtime leader of the United Farm Workers' Labor Union, has died.
And Piers Adrian Florido reports in the '60s and '70s she led strikes and boycotts to improve working conditions for Mexican-American agricultural workers.
In the 1960s, Huerta co-founded the union that would become the United Farm Workers with Cesar Chavez.
She became a fierce organizer, urging low-paid Mexican-American farmhands to strike for better working conditions.
She was a driving force in the UFW's national boycott of table grapes.
It pressured California grape growers to sign the country's first major labor contracts for farm workers.
She left the union in the early 2000s and broadened her activism, training young organizers and advocating for immigrant rights.
Earlier this year, she told the New York Times that decades ago Cesar Chavez had raped her.
She said she spoke out in solidarity with other women who'd come forward with credible accounts of child sexual assault by the revered labor activist.
Adrian Florido, NPR News.
The hand-drawn chart of the Mason-Dixon line that eventually divided the free and slave states is up for auction.
Originally intended to settle a border dispute between the colonies of Maryland and Pennsylvania,
Charles Mason's and Jeremiah Dixon's survey became synonymous with the divisions that exploded into civil war four decades later.
This is NPR News from Washington.

Midwest voters feel squeezed by rising costs as affordability becomes a midterm issue
Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady, expected to raise them later this year
Minnesota man Salim Saeed sentenced to 30 years for defrauding federal food program
Dolores Huerta, co-founder of United Farm Workers union, dies at age of 95
